newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to include China in economic zone plan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to include China in economic zone plan.

text.p: Taiwan's top economic policymaking body said on Saturday it will still include rival China in its planned special economic zones that will allow unfettered economic activities by foreign investors.

"The planned zones will adopt a global point of view, including mainland China," an official at the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development quoted council chairman Chiang Pin-kung as concluding the first minister-level, ad hoc meeting for the plan.
"Regarding ties with mainland China in the special zones, we'll adopt cautious, practical, mutually beneficial and step-by-step principles," Chiang was quoted as saying.
This contradicted an unconfirmed October 1996 state-run Central News Agency report that the island would initially exclude China from the planned special zones.
The planned special economic zones, where free exchanges in personnel, information, liquidity and goods will be allowed, will be open to foreign countries.
Although all investments in China must be government approved, Taiwan remains concerned its economy may become too dependent on China, and thus politically vulnerable.

Taiwan officials, including President Lee Teng-hui, regularly accuse China of using commerce as a political lever against the island, and have urged local businesses to slow their mainland investments.
State television on Saturday quoted Chiang as telling a news conference that the government plans to choose the southern harbour of Kaohsiung as the first test area for the zones.

"We'll mainly utilise major harbours and international airports for the special zones, so we'll also consider using (the central) Taichung Harbour and (the northern) Taoyuan airport city," Chiang said on state television. Facing increasing economic ties with China, Taiwan has said it would allow direct transport links with China through certain special economic zones in Taiwan.
Taiwan has banned direct contact with China after a civil war ended in 1949. All trade with and investment in China must be conducted through a third region, mostly Hong Kong.

Despite the ban on direct links, indirect commerce has flourished since the late 1980s when political tensions started to thaw. Some 30,000 Taiwanese firms have poured more than US$20 billion into China so far.
The island has hoped the special economic zones would help Taiwan fulfill its ambition to become a regional operation hub for Asia-Pacific transnational companies.
